categoryBlurb: Real chiles toasted on a dry pan, tortillas warmed one at a time, and pots that fill the whole apartment with the smell of orange peel and cumin — this is the chapter that turns a weeknight into a taco night and a free Saturday into something worth remembering.

recipes.title: Carne Asada Tacos with Salsa Verde
recipes.blurb: Thin skirt steak marinated in citrus and garlic, charred hard and fast, then chopped small and piled into warm corn tortillas with a bright tomatillo salsa. This is the taco that makes people ask what you did differently.

items: 2 lb (900 g) skirt steak or flank steak, trimmed
1/3 cup (80 ml) fresh orange juice (about 1 large orange)
1/4 cup (60 ml) fresh lime juice (about 3 limes)
1/4 cup (60 ml) neutral oil, such as avocado or canola
1 jalapeno, seeded and minced (about 2 tbsp / 15 g)
1/2 cup (20 g) chopped cilantro, leaves and stems
1 lb (450 g) tomatillos (about 8 medium), husked and rinsed
2 serrano chiles, stemmed (or 1 jalapeno for less heat)
1/2 white onion, cut into 2 thick wedges (about 4 oz / 115 g)
1/2 cup (20 g) cilantro leaves and tender stems
1 tsp (6 g) kosher salt, plus more to taste
1/2 white onion, finely diced (about 3/4 cup / 110 g)

instructions.title: Trim and portion the steak
instructions.text: Skirt steak arrives as a long rope with a thin silvery membrane and pockets of hard fat, so shave those away with a paring knife — they never render and they turn chewy. Cut the 2 lb (900 g) piece crosswise into 3 or 4 lengths of about 8 in (20 cm) so each piece fits flat in your pan or on the grill. Short pieces are much easier to flip and, more importantly, easier to slice against the grain later. Pat everything dry with paper towels so the marinade clings instead of sliding off.

instructions.title: Mix the marinade
instructions.text: Whisk together the orange juice, lime juice, oil, garlic, jalapeno, cilantro, cumin, chili powder, oregano, 1 tbsp kosher salt and the black pepper in a bowl. Orange juice is not there for sweetness — its gentler acid tenderizes the meat without turning the surface chalky and mushy the way straight lime does over hours. Taste it: it should be aggressively salty and sour, because only a thin film of it ends up on the steak.

instructions.title: Marinate 2 to 8 hours
instructions.text: Put the steak in a zip-top bag or a shallow dish, pour the marinade over, and press out the air so the liquid touches every surface. Refrigerate for at least 2 hours and no more than 8 — past that window the citrus starts breaking the muscle fibers down into something soft and pasty. Turn the bag once halfway through if you think of it. This is the one step you cannot rush, so start it in the morning if dinner is at seven.

instructions.title: Char the salsa vegetables
instructions.text: Arrange the tomatillos, serranos, onion wedges and unpeeled garlic on a foil-lined sheet pan and slide it 4 in (10 cm) under a preheated broiler. Broil for 8 to 10 minutes, turning everything once, until the tomatillos slump and blister and go from bright green to a dull olive with blackened patches. That char is where the smoky depth comes from, so let them get genuinely spotted black, not just soft. Pull the garlic early if the skins are burning and squeeze the cloves out of their papers.

instructions.title: Blend the salsa verde
instructions.text: Scrape the vegetables and every drop of juice from the pan into a blender, add the cilantro, lime juice and 1 tsp salt, and pulse 8 to 10 times. You want a loose, slightly chunky salsa, not a smooth green milkshake — over-blending whips in air and turns it pale and foamy. Taste and add salt a pinch at a time until the flavor snaps into focus. It will taste sharper hot than cold, so let it cool for 10 minutes before you judge it.

instructions.title: Take the steak out early
instructions.text: Pull the steak from the fridge 30 minutes before cooking and let it sit on the counter. Lift each piece out of the marinade and scrape off the garlic and cilantro bits with the back of a knife — solids like these burn black and bitter over high heat. Then pat both sides thoroughly dry with paper towels. A wet steak steams and stays gray; a dry one browns in seconds.

instructions.title: Get the fire screaming hot
instructions.text: Build a hot charcoal fire or set a gas grill to high, or heat a 12 in (30 cm) cast iron skillet over high heat for 4 to 5 minutes indoors. You want it hot enough that a drop of water vanishes instantly with a hiss. Skirt steak is only about 1/2 in (1.3 cm) thick, so it needs a ferocious surface temperature to build a crust before the inside overcooks. If you are indoors, turn the vent on high and open a window now, not later.

instructions.title: Sear hard and fast
instructions.text: Lay the steak down and leave it completely alone for 3 to 4 minutes — it should sizzle loudly and steadily, not smoke black. Flip once and give it 2 to 3 minutes on the second side, until an instant-read thermometer in the thickest part reads 130°F (54°C) for medium-rare. Work in batches if the pieces are crowding each other, because crowding drops the pan temperature and you get gray meat. Skirt steak goes from perfect to leathery in about 90 seconds, so keep the thermometer in your hand.

instructions.title: Rest the steak
instructions.text: Move the steak to a cutting board and let it rest for 8 to 10 minutes, loosely tented with foil. During the rest the internal temperature coasts up to about 135°F (57°C) and the juices that were driven to the center redistribute through the meat. Cut into it too early and half of that liquid runs onto the board instead of staying in the taco. Use this time to warm the tortillas.

instructions.title: Warm the tortillas
instructions.text: Heat a dry comal or skillet over medium-high and toast each corn tortilla for 20 to 30 seconds per side, until it is pliable, smells toasty, and puffs slightly in spots. Stack the warm ones inside a clean kitchen towel so they steam each other soft. Cold tortillas crack and taste like cardboard, and this step takes four minutes. For street-style tacos, double up two tortillas per taco so nothing falls through.

instructions.title: Chop against the grain
instructions.text: Look for the long parallel muscle fibers running across each piece of skirt steak — they are easy to see on this cut. Slice across them into thin strips, then turn the strips and chop them into rough 1/2 in (1.3 cm) pieces. Cutting with the grain instead of across it is the single most common reason carne asada comes out tough. Pour any juices from the board back over the chopped meat.

instructions.title: Build and eat immediately
instructions.text: Pile a generous 1/4 cup of chopped steak into each warm tortilla, then top with diced white onion, chopped cilantro, and a big spoonful of salsa verde. Finish with a hard squeeze of lime right before it goes in your mouth — the acid wakes the whole thing up. Tacos wait for no one, so serve them straight off the board with the salsa bowl in the middle of the table.

tips: Skirt steak beats flank here because its loose grain grabs marinade and it cooks in half the time. If you can only find flank, slice it thinner and expect an extra minute per side.
The salsa verde keeps in the fridge for 5 days and only gets better on day two. Make a double batch and put it on eggs.

No broiler? Char the tomatillos and chiles in a dry cast iron skillet over medium-high heat for 10 to 12 minutes, turning until blackened in patches. The result is slightly more toasty and less juicy, which is not a bad thing.
If the salsa tastes harsh or metallic, it needs salt, not more lime. Tomatillos are acidic enough on their own.
Corn tortillas from a Mexican market are worth the detour. Warm them on the comal the moment before serving, not ten minutes ahead.
recipes.keyTemp: Pull skirt or flank steak at 130°F (54°C) for medium-rare; it coasts to about 135°F (57°C) as it rests. Past 145°F (63°C) these thin cuts turn tough and dry.
recipes.pairing: A cold Mexican lager with lime, or a salty Tommy's margarita, with charro beans and Mexican rice alongside.

recipes.title: Chicken Tinga Tostadas
recipes.blurb: Shredded chicken simmered in a smoky chipotle and tomato sauce until it soaks up every bit of it, spooned onto crisp tostadas with beans and crema. It is a weeknight dinner that tastes like it took all afternoon.

items: 2 lb (900 g) boneless skinless chicken thighs
1/2 white onion, left in one piece (about 4 oz / 115 g)
1 white onion, thinly sliced (about 1 1/2 cups / 200 g)
3 chipotle chiles in adobo, plus 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the adobo sauce
1 cup (240 ml) reserved chicken poaching broth
1 tsp (6 g) kosher salt, plus more to taste
1/2 cup (120 ml) Mexican crema or thinned sour cream

instructions.title: Poach the chicken
instructions.text: Put the thighs, onion half, garlic cloves, bay leaf and 1 tbsp salt in a saucepan and add the 6 cups (1.4 L) water, which should cover everything by an inch. Bring it to a bare simmer over medium-high heat, then immediately drop it to low so the surface only shivers with a bubble every second or two. A hard boil squeezes the thighs tight and dry, while a gentle poach leaves them silky. Cook for 18 to 20 minutes, until an instant-read thermometer in the thickest thigh reads 165°F (74°C).

instructions.title: Cool and shred
instructions.text: Lift the chicken out with tongs onto a plate and let it sit for 10 minutes so it is cool enough to handle and the fibers relax. Save 1 cup (240 ml) of the poaching broth and strain the rest into a jar for another day — it is far better than anything from a box. Pull the meat apart with two forks or your fingers into rough shreds about the width of a pencil. Leave them a little chunky; wispy shreds disappear into the sauce instead of holding onto it.

instructions.title: Blanch and peel the tomatoes
instructions.text: Bring a small pot of water to a boil, cut a shallow X in the bottom of each Roma tomato, and drop them in for 45 to 60 seconds. Move them to a bowl of cold water and the skins will slip off with your thumb. Peeling matters here because tomato skins roll up into little leathery curls in a simmered sauce. If you would rather skip it, use one 28 oz (794 g) can of whole peeled tomatoes, drained, which is the equivalent of 1 1/2 lb of fresh.

instructions.title: Blend the tomato base
instructions.text: Put the peeled tomatoes, chipotles, adobo sauce, oregano and cumin in a blender and run it for 30 seconds until completely smooth. Start with 2 chipotles if you are heat-shy — you can always stir a third in later, but you cannot take it out. The blended sauce should be the color of brick and smell distinctly smoky, not just tomatoey. Set it right next to the stove.

instructions.title: Sweat the onions properly
instructions.text: Heat the 2 tbsp oil in a 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium heat, add the sliced onion, and cook for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring every couple of minutes. You are after soft, sweet, translucent onions with just a few golden edges, not crunchy ones — this is where the sauce gets its backbone. Add the sliced garlic in the last minute so it perfumes the oil without burning. Burnt garlic turns the whole pan bitter and there is no fixing it.

instructions.title: Fry the sauce
instructions.text: Pour the blended tomato mixture into the hot skillet all at once — it should hiss and spit, so stand back. Cook it hard for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring often, until it darkens a shade, thickens noticeably, and a spoon dragged through the pan leaves a trail that holds for a second. Frying the puree cooks off the raw tomato edge and concentrates everything. Skipping this step is why homemade tinga sometimes tastes thin and sour.

instructions.title: Simmer the chicken in the sauce
instructions.text: Stir in the shredded chicken and the reserved 1 cup (240 ml) broth, then bring it back to a gentle simmer. Cook uncovered for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring now and then, until the liquid reduces and clings to the meat instead of pooling in the pan. The chicken should look glossy and coated, not soupy. Add the 1 tsp salt, taste, and adjust — poached chicken drinks up more salt than you expect.

instructions.title: Warm the beans and tostadas
instructions.text: Heat the refried beans in a small pan over low with a splash of water until they are spreadable and loose, about 5 minutes. Crisp the tostada shells in a 350°F (175°C) oven for 3 to 4 minutes if they came from a bag and taste stale. Warm shells and warm beans hold up much better under a wet topping. Have everything ready before you assemble, because tostadas soften fast.

instructions.title: Build the tostadas
instructions.text: Spread about 2 tbsp of refried beans on each tostada all the way to the edge — the beans are the glue that keeps the topping from sliding off. Pile on a generous 1/3 cup of the hot tinga, then add sliced avocado, a shower of queso fresco, and a drizzle of crema. Finish with a squeeze of lime. Assemble them one at a time as people eat, not in a big batch on a tray.

instructions.title: Serve with the pot on the table
instructions.text: Bring the skillet of tinga right to the table with a spoon in it and let everyone build their own. Leftover tinga is even better the next day once the smoke settles into the meat. It reheats in a covered pan over low with a splash of water, about 5 minutes. Anything left after that goes into quesadillas or over rice.

tips: Chicken thighs are the right call here — breasts turn stringy after ten minutes of simmering in sauce. If you only have breasts, poach them to 165°F (74°C) and stir them in during the last 4 minutes.
Freeze leftover chipotles in adobo in a small container in single-chile portions; a can goes bad long before you use it up.
Tinga freezes beautifully for up to 3 months. Cool it completely, then freeze flat in a zip-top bag and thaw overnight in the fridge.
If it comes out too spicy, stir in 2 tbsp of crema or a spoonful of the refried beans directly into the pan — the fat blunts the capsaicin.
The same tinga makes excellent tacos, quesadillas or a topping for baked potatoes. Make a double batch on Sunday.
recipes.keyTemp: Chicken is safely cooked at 165°F (74°C) checked in the thickest part of a thigh. It then simmers in the sauce, which will not dry it out because thighs hold moisture well.
recipes.pairing: Mexican rice and a cold agua fresca de jamaica, or a light lager if you want something with bubbles.

recipes.title: Michoacan-Style Pork Carnitas
recipes.blurb: Pork shoulder simmered slow in its own fat with orange and cinnamon, then crisped under high heat until the edges shatter and the middle stays juicy. This is the one worth clearing an afternoon for.

items: 4 lb (1.8 kg) boneless pork shoulder (Boston butt), cut into 2 in (5 cm) chunks
1/2 cup (110 g) lard, or 1/2 cup (120 ml) neutral oil
1 orange, halved (juice squeezed in, spent halves added too)
1 white onion, finely diced (about 1 1/2 cups / 220 g)
1 cup (240 ml) salsa verde or salsa roja

instructions.title: Cut the pork the right size
instructions.text: Cut the shoulder into 2 in (5 cm) chunks and leave the fat cap on — do not trim it, because that fat is the entire point of carnitas. Pieces this size hold their shape through a long braise and still develop plenty of surface area for crisping later. Anything smaller falls into threads before the connective tissue melts. Pat the chunks dry so the seasoning sticks.

instructions.title: Season and let it sit
instructions.text: Toss the pork with the 1 tbsp kosher salt, black pepper, cumin and Mexican oregano until every piece is coated. Let it stand at room temperature for 15 minutes while you get everything else ready, which gives the salt time to start working into the surface. Mexican oregano is more citrusy and less minty than Mediterranean oregano and is worth seeking out. If you only have the Italian kind, use half as much.

instructions.title: Melt the lard and start the braise
instructions.text: Melt the 1/2 cup (110 g) lard in a large heavy Dutch oven over medium heat, then add the pork in a single layer or as close as you can get. Squeeze the orange halves over the pot and drop the spent shells in, then add the onion, garlic, bay leaves, cinnamon stick, milk and the 2 cups (475 ml) water. The liquid should come about halfway up the pork, not cover it — top up with a splash more water if your pot is wide and the pork looks stranded. This is a confit, not a stew — the pork mostly cooks in fat with just enough liquid to keep the bottom from scorching.

instructions.title: Simmer low and slow
instructions.text: Bring the pot to a simmer, then turn the heat to low so you see a lazy bubble breaking the surface every second or so. Cover partially with the lid set askew and cook for 2 hours to 2 hours 30 minutes, stirring gently every 30 minutes. Resist the urge to crank the heat: a hard boil tightens the muscle fibers and gives you dry, stringy pork instead of meltingly soft chunks. The kitchen will smell like orange peel and pork fat, which is exactly right.

instructions.title: Check for doneness by feel
instructions.text: The pork is ready when a piece offers no resistance to a fork and pulls apart into large shreds under gentle pressure, at an internal temperature of about 200°F (93°C). Do not rely on the clock alone, because a well-marbled shoulder can take 30 minutes longer than a lean one. If it still feels springy or tight, give it another 20 minutes and check again. Undercooked carnitas is the most common failure and it cannot be fixed at the crisping stage.

instructions.title: Boil off the liquid
instructions.text: Fish out and discard the onion, garlic, bay leaves, cinnamon stick and orange shells with tongs. Raise the heat to medium and let the remaining liquid bubble away for 10 to 15 minutes until only clear fat and a little browned sediment are left in the pot. You will hear the sound shift from a wet gurgle to a sharp sizzle — that is the water gone and the frying starting. From here on, the pork is essentially deep-frying in its own rendered fat.

instructions.title: Rest before crisping
instructions.text: Lift the chunks onto a rimmed sheet pan with a slotted spoon and let them rest for 10 minutes, which firms them up enough to handle. Pour 3 to 4 tbsp of the rendered fat from the pot over the pork and save the rest in a jar for beans or eggs. Gently press each chunk with the back of a spoon to flatten it slightly, exposing more surface. More surface means more crispy edges, which is the whole reason anyone loves carnitas.

instructions.title: Crisp under the broiler
instructions.text: Set an oven rack 6 in (15 cm) below the broiler element and turn the broiler to high. Broil the pork for 4 to 6 minutes, until the tops are deep brown and crackling at the edges. Watch it constantly — the line between crisp and burnt is about 45 seconds under a broiler. Alternatively, crisp the pork in batches in a hot cast iron skillet over medium-high heat for 3 to 4 minutes per side.

instructions.title: Flip and finish
instructions.text: Pull the pan out, turn the pieces with tongs, and broil for another 3 to 4 minutes so the second side browns too. You are aiming for roughly half crisp, golden-brown exterior and half soft, juicy interior, not uniformly crunchy pork. If some pieces are done before others, move them to the edges of the pan where the heat is less direct. Give it all a squeeze of lime while it is still on the hot pan.

instructions.title: Chop and dress
instructions.text: Roughly chop or pull the crisped pork on a board, keeping some big shaggy pieces for texture. Drizzle a few tablespoons of the hot rendered fat and pan juices back over the top and toss once — that is the seasoning. Taste and add a pinch of salt if it needs it. Serve straight from the board while everything is still crackling.

instructions.title: Warm the tortillas and build
instructions.text: Toast the corn tortillas on a dry comal or skillet over medium-high heat for 20 to 30 seconds per side, then stack them in a towel to stay soft. Fill each with about 1/3 cup of carnitas, then top with diced white onion, cilantro, salsa and a hard squeeze of lime. Two tortillas per taco is standard for anything this juicy. Put the bowls in the middle of the table and let everyone go.

tips: Lard makes noticeably better carnitas than oil and is sold cheaply at any Mexican grocery. Strain and refrigerate what is left over — it keeps for months and makes the best refried beans you will ever eat.

The milk is not optional folklore; its sugars and proteins help the pork brown and add a subtle richness. It will look curdled during the braise, which is normal and disappears when you boil the liquid off.
You can braise the pork up to 3 days ahead and refrigerate it in its fat. Crisp it under the broiler straight from the fridge, adding 2 extra minutes.
If your pork tastes flat after crisping, it needs salt and acid, in that order. A pinch of salt and a squeeze of lime fixes almost every batch.
Leftovers make outstanding breakfast: crisp them again in a skillet and top with two fried eggs and salsa verde.
recipes.keyTemp: Braise the pork to about 200°F (93°C), far past the 145°F (63°C) plus a 3-minute rest that pork needs for safety, because that is where the collagen turns to gelatin and the meat shreds. Judge it by fork tenderness, not the clock.
recipes.pairing: A Mexican lager or a michelada, with refried beans and pickled red onions on the side.

recipes.title: Baja Fish Tacos with Cabbage Slaw
recipes.blurb: Beer-battered white fish that stays shatteringly crisp under a pile of lime-cut cabbage and chipotle crema. It is the taco stand in Ensenada, made in your kitchen in under an hour.

items: 1 1/2 lb (680 g) cod, halibut or mahi mahi, cut into strips 1 in x 4 in (2.5 cm x 10 cm)
1 cup (120 g) all-purpose flour, plus 1/2 cup (60 g) for dredging
1 tsp (6 g) kosher salt, for the batter
1 tsp (6 g) kosher salt, for seasoning the fish and the fried strips
8 cups (1.9 L) neutral oil, for frying
4 cups (280 g) green cabbage, shredded very thin
1/4 red onion, sliced paper thin (about 1/2 cup / 60 g)
1/2 cup (120 g) Mexican crema or sour cream
1 chipotle in adobo, minced, plus 1 tsp adobo sauce

instructions.title: Salt the cabbage first
instructions.text: Toss the shredded cabbage and red onion with the 1 tsp salt and 2 tbsp lime juice in a bowl and let it sit for at least 20 minutes while you do everything else. The salt pulls water out of the cabbage so it stays crunchy instead of going limp on the taco, and the lime softens the raw bite of the onion. Squeeze the slaw gently with your hands before serving and pour off the liquid that collects. Stir in the cilantro at the last minute so it stays green.

instructions.title: Make the chipotle crema
instructions.text: Whisk the crema, mayonnaise, 2 tbsp lime juice, minced chipotle, adobo sauce and 1/2 tsp salt in a small bowl until smooth. It should be thin enough to drizzle from a spoon in a steady ribbon; add water 1 tsp at a time if it is too thick. Taste it and remember it will be competing with fried fish, so it needs to be assertively tangy and a little spicy. Refrigerate until serving.

instructions.title: Cut and dry the fish
instructions.text: Cut the fillets into strips about 1 in (2.5 cm) wide and 4 in (10 cm) long, roughly the width of two fingers, so they cook through in the same time it takes the batter to brown. Blot every piece dry on paper towels and season them lightly with half of the 1 tsp of salt set aside for the fish, saving the rest for after they come out of the oil. Wet fish makes the batter slide right off in the oil. Keep the fish in the fridge until the oil is at temperature.

instructions.title: Heat the oil to 375°F
instructions.text: Pour the 8 cups (1.9 L) of oil into a heavy 5 to 6 qt Dutch oven, which gives you a depth of about 1 1/2 in (4 cm) — enough for the strips to float free without the pot being dangerously full — and clip a thermometer to the side. Heat over medium-high to 375°F (190°C), which usually takes 8 to 10 minutes. Starting high matters because adding cold fish drops the oil by 25 to 50 degrees, and you want to land near 350°F (175°C) while frying. Oil below 325°F (163°C) gives you greasy, pale batter every time.

instructions.title: Mix the batter at the last second
instructions.text: Whisk the 1 cup (120 g) flour, cornstarch, baking powder, the 1 tsp of batter salt, garlic powder and chili powder in a bowl, then pour in the cold beer and stir just until it comes together with a few small lumps left. Overmixing develops gluten and gives you a bready, tough coating instead of a crisp shell. The batter should be about the thickness of heavy cream and drip off a spoon in a slow ribbon. Mix it right before frying so the bubbles are still lively.

instructions.title: Dredge, then batter
instructions.text: Put the extra 1/2 cup (65 g) flour in a shallow dish and toss each fish strip in it, shaking off the excess. That dry layer gives the wet batter something to grip so it does not slip off in the fryer. Dip a floured strip into the batter, let the excess run off for a count of two, then lower it into the oil away from you. Do not batter the fish ahead of time; do it one piece at a time as you fry.

instructions.title: Fry in small batches
instructions.text: Fry 3 or 4 strips at a time for 3 to 4 minutes total, turning once, until the coating is deep golden and audibly crisp when tapped with tongs. Crowding the pot drops the oil temperature and the batter absorbs oil instead of crisping. Let the oil come back up to 375°F (190°C) between batches, which takes about a minute. The fish is done at an internal temperature of 145°F (63°C) and will flake easily.

instructions.title: Drain on a rack, not paper
instructions.text: Lift each piece onto a wire rack set over a sheet pan and sprinkle immediately with the remaining 1/2 tsp of fish salt while the surface is still glistening — salt only sticks to hot, oily batter. A rack lets air circulate underneath so the bottom stays crisp; paper towels trap steam and the coating goes soft in two minutes. If you are frying several batches, keep the finished fish in a 200°F (95°C) oven. Never stack fried fish on top of itself.

instructions.title: Warm the tortillas
instructions.text: Toast the corn tortillas on a dry skillet or comal over medium-high heat for 20 to 30 seconds a side, until they are soft, flexible and smell like toasted corn. Wrap them in a clean towel to hold the steam and keep them warm. Warm tortillas fold without cracking and taste dramatically better than microwaved ones. Get these ready while the last batch of fish fries.

instructions.title: Build the tacos
instructions.text: Lay one or two pieces of fish in each warm tortilla, then top with a small handful of drained slaw, a heavy drizzle of chipotle crema, and a sprinkle of cotija. Squeeze a lime wedge over the top just before eating. Build them one at a time and eat them standing at the counter if necessary — the batter is at its best for about 90 seconds. Put the extra crema on the table for dipping.

tips: Cod is the classic choice and the most forgiving, but any firm white fish works. Avoid thin, delicate fillets like sole, which fall apart in the batter.
The beer must be cold and carbonated. The bubbles are what make the coating light, so open it right before you mix.
For a lighter version, skip the batter entirely: season the fish with chili powder and cumin and sear it in a hot skillet for 2 to 3 minutes per side to 145°F (63°C).
Slaw and crema both hold in the fridge for 2 days, so you can prep them in the morning and only fry at dinner.
Save the frying oil: cool it completely, strain it through a coffee filter, and it is good for two more fish fries.
recipes.keyTemp: Fish is cooked through at 145°F (63°C) and will flake with gentle pressure. Keep the frying oil between 350°F (175°C) and 375°F (190°C) throughout.
recipes.pairing: A cold Pacifico with lime, or a grapefruit paloma, with a pile of tortilla chips and salsa to start.

recipes.title: Chiles Rellenos in Tomato Caldillo
recipes.blurb: Charred poblanos stuffed with melting cheese, wrapped in a cloud-light egg batter, fried golden and set in a simple tomato broth. It takes patience and it is absolutely worth it.

items: 6 large poblano chiles (about 1 1/2 lb / 680 g total)
12 oz (340 g) Oaxaca cheese or Monterey Jack, cut into batons 3 in (8 cm) long
1 cup (240 ml) chicken or vegetable broth
3/4 tsp (5 g) kosher salt, plus more to taste
4 large eggs, separated, at room temperature
2 tbsp (15 g) all-purpose flour, for the batter
1/2 cup (60 g) all-purpose flour, for dusting
4 cups (950 ml) neutral oil, for frying

instructions.title: Char the poblanos
instructions.text: Set the poblanos directly over a high gas flame, or on a sheet pan 4 in (10 cm) under a hot broiler, and turn them every 2 to 3 minutes with tongs. You want the skin blistered and blackened over roughly 80 percent of each chile, which takes 8 to 12 minutes total. Do not rush this by cranking the heat higher — you are trying to blister the skin without cooking the flesh to mush. The chiles should still feel firm when you pick them up.

instructions.title: Steam and peel
instructions.text: Pile the hot chiles into a bowl and cover it tightly with plastic wrap or a plate for 10 to 15 minutes so they steam in their own heat. The trapped moisture separates the skin from the flesh and it will slip off under your thumb. Peel them with your fingers, not under running water, which washes away the smoky flavor you just spent ten minutes building. A few stubborn black flecks left behind are fine and traditional.

instructions.title: Open and seed carefully
instructions.text: Lay each chile flat and cut a single 3 in (8 cm) slit down one side, stopping about 1/2 in (1.3 cm) from the stem and the tip. Reach in with a small spoon or your fingers and pull out the seed pod and any loose seeds, keeping the chile otherwise intact. This is the delicate part: a tear means cheese leaking into the oil later. Sprinkle the inside of each with a pinch of the 1/2 tsp salt.

instructions.title: Stuff and secure
instructions.text: Slide 2 oz (55 g) of cheese batons into each chile, filling it generously but not so full that the slit gapes open. Press the edges of the slit together and pin them closed with a toothpick woven through like a stitch. Set the stuffed chiles on a plate and refrigerate for 15 minutes so the cheese firms up. Cold cheese takes longer to melt and run, which buys you time in the fryer.

instructions.title: Make the caldillo
instructions.text: Blend the tomatoes, onion and garlic until smooth, about 30 seconds. Heat the 1 tbsp oil in a saucepan over medium-high, pour in the puree — it will hiss — and cook for 5 minutes, stirring, until it darkens slightly. Add the broth, oregano and 3/4 tsp salt and simmer for 10 minutes until it is the consistency of a thin soup that lightly coats a spoon. Taste and adjust the salt; keep it warm over low heat.

instructions.title: Heat the frying oil
instructions.text: Pour the 4 cups (950 ml) oil into a 10 in (25 cm) skillet or wide saucepan, which gives a depth of about 3/4 in (2 cm), and heat over medium to 350°F (175°C). That is shallow on purpose: chiles rellenos are basted with hot oil rather than submerged, so the puffed batter never gets pressed flat against the pan. Use a thermometer — this batter is unforgiving. Too cool and it soaks up oil and slides off; too hot and the outside browns before the cheese melts. While it heats, set a wire rack over a sheet pan next to the stove.

instructions.title: Beat the whites to stiff peaks
instructions.text: Beat the 4 egg whites in a clean, completely dry bowl with a mixer on medium-high for 3 to 4 minutes, until they hold a stiff peak that stands straight up when you lift the beater. Any speck of yolk or drop of water will keep them from whipping, so wipe the bowl with a little vinegar first if you are unsure. Stiff peaks are what make the coating puff into a golden cloud. Underwhipped whites give you a flat, eggy pancake.

instructions.title: Fold in the yolks
instructions.text: Add the 2 tbsp flour and 1/2 tsp salt to the whites and fold twice, then add the yolks and fold gently with a spatula just until no streaks of yellow remain, about 10 strokes. Cut down through the middle, sweep along the bottom, and turn the mixture over rather than stirring in circles. Every extra stroke deflates the air you just whipped in. Use the batter within 5 minutes; it will not wait.

instructions.title: Dust the chiles with flour
instructions.text: Spread the 1/2 cup (65 g) flour on a plate and roll each stuffed chile in it, patting off all but a thin film. Dry flour is the bridge between the wet chile skin and the egg batter, and skipping it is the number one reason the coating slides off in the oil. Hold each chile by the stem when you dust it. Have them all floured and lined up before you start frying.

instructions.title: Batter and fry
instructions.text: Holding a chile by the stem, lower it into the egg batter and spoon batter over it until it is completely coated, then lay it gently into the 350°F (175°C) oil away from you. Fry 2 at a time for 2 to 3 minutes, spooning hot oil over the top with a spoon so the exposed side sets. Flip carefully with two spoons and fry another 2 minutes until deep golden all over. Crowding the pan makes them stick together and tear.

instructions.title: Drain and rest
instructions.text: Lift each chile onto the wire rack with a slotted spoon and let it drain for 2 minutes while you fry the rest. A rack keeps the bottom crisp; a paper towel steams it soft. Pull the toothpicks out now while you can still see them. Sprinkle with a small pinch of salt while they are hot.

instructions.title: Serve in the caldillo
instructions.text: Ladle about 1/2 cup of the warm tomato caldillo into each shallow bowl and set one or two chiles on top so the batter stays crisp above the sauce rather than drowning in it. Serve immediately — chiles rellenos are a dish you eat the minute they are done, not one you hold. Pass extra caldillo and warm tortillas at the table. Warn everyone that the cheese inside is molten hot.

tips: Oaxaca cheese is the right one: it melts into stretchy strands rather than breaking into grease the way cheddar does. Low-moisture mozzarella is a decent substitute.
You can char, peel and stuff the chiles up to a day ahead and keep them covered in the fridge. Only the batter and the frying have to happen at the last minute.
If the batter slides off during frying, the chiles were wet or under-floured. Pat them dry before dusting and use a light but complete coat of flour.
Poblanos vary in heat from mild to genuinely spicy and there is no way to tell from the outside. Taste a fleck of one after peeling so you know what you are serving.
Traditional versions add shredded picadillo instead of cheese. If you have leftover carnitas or tinga, mix 1 cup of it with the cheese for a heartier chile.
recipes.keyTemp: Keep the frying oil at 350°F (175°C) — the batter needs that exact window to puff and set. The chiles are ready when the cheese inside is fully molten, around 160°F (71°C) in the center.
recipes.pairing: Mexican rice and black beans, with a crisp lager or a glass of dry Mexican rosé.

recipes.title: Chicken Enchiladas Verdes
recipes.blurb: Tomatillo salsa with real heat and real acid, poured over chicken-filled corn tortillas and baked until the cheese blisters. Tangy, green and much brighter than any red enchilada.

items: 2 lb (900 g) tomatillos (about 16 medium), husked and rinsed
1 cup (40 g) cilantro leaves and tender stems
1 1/2 tsp (9 g) kosher salt, plus more to taste
3 cups (450 g) cooked shredded chicken, from a rotisserie bird or 2 poached breasts
1/4 cup (60 ml) neutral oil, for softening the tortillas
8 oz (225 g) Monterey Jack or Oaxaca cheese, shredded (about 2 cups)
1/2 cup (120 ml) Mexican crema or thinned sour cream
1/2 small white onion, sliced paper thin (about 1/2 cup / 70 g)

instructions.title: Char the tomatillos and chiles
instructions.text: Spread the tomatillos, serranos, onion halves and unpeeled garlic on a foil-lined sheet pan and broil 4 in (10 cm) from the element for 8 to 10 minutes, turning once. The tomatillos should slump, blister and turn from bright green to olive with blackened patches. That char is the difference between a salsa that tastes flat and one that tastes like a taqueria. Pull the garlic as soon as its skin is browned and squeeze the soft cloves free.

instructions.title: Blend the salsa
instructions.text: Scrape everything, including all the juices on the pan, into a blender with the cilantro and blend until smooth, about 45 seconds. It will look pale and foamy right out of the blender, which is normal and disappears once it is cooked. Start with 2 serranos if you are cautious; tomatillo salsa hides its heat until the third bite. Do not add salt yet.

instructions.title: Fry the salsa
instructions.text: Heat the 1 tbsp oil in a large saucepan over medium-high until it shimmers, then pour in the blended salsa all at once and stand back from the spitting. Cook for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring often, until it darkens to a deeper green and thickens enough to coat a spoon. Frying the salsa is what turns a raw, sharp puree into a rounded sauce. Add the chicken broth and 1 1/2 tsp salt and simmer 5 more minutes.

instructions.title: Season the chicken
instructions.text: Toss the 3 cups shredded chicken with 1/2 cup of the warm salsa verde and the 1/2 tsp salt in a bowl. Moistening the filling now keeps it from drying out in the oven and means every bite has sauce in it, not just on it. Use thigh meat if you can — it stays juicy through baking where breast meat can go chalky. Taste it; the filling should be seasoned enough to eat on its own.

instructions.title: Heat the oven
instructions.text: Preheat the oven to 400°F (205°C) and set a rack in the middle. Spread 3/4 cup of the salsa verde across the bottom of a 9 x 13 in (23 x 33 cm) baking dish in a thin, even layer. That base layer keeps the tortillas from sticking and gluing themselves to the dish. Have the dish, the filling, the cheese and the salsa all lined up before you start rolling.

instructions.title: Soften the tortillas in oil
instructions.text: Heat the 1/4 cup (60 ml) oil in a small skillet over medium until it shimmers, then slip in one tortilla at a time for about 10 seconds per side. It should turn pliable and slightly puffy but never crisp. This quick fry is the traditional step everyone skips, and it is why restaurant enchiladas hold together while home versions dissolve into mush. Drain each tortilla on paper towels and stack them as you go.

instructions.title: Dip and roll
instructions.text: Dip a softened tortilla into the pot of warm salsa verde so both sides are lightly coated, then lay it on a plate. Spoon about 1/4 cup of chicken down the center, add a small pinch of cheese, and roll it up snugly. Place it seam side down in the baking dish and repeat, nestling each one against the last. Working assembly-line style keeps your hands from getting hopelessly sticky.

instructions.title: Sauce and cheese
instructions.text: Pour the remaining salsa verde evenly over the rolled enchiladas, making sure the ends are covered because exposed tortilla edges turn to leather in the oven. Scatter the shredded cheese over the top in an even layer. Do not drown them — you want the tops sitting just at the surface of the sauce, not submerged. A little sauce should pool at the sides.

instructions.title: Bake until bubbling
instructions.text: Bake uncovered for 18 to 22 minutes, until the sauce bubbles vigorously around the edges and the cheese is fully melted with a few golden-brown blisters. If the cheese has melted but not browned, run the dish under the broiler for 60 to 90 seconds, watching it constantly. The center of the dish should register 165°F (74°C) on a thermometer. The bubbling is your real cue, not the clock.

instructions.title: Rest before serving
instructions.text: Let the dish sit on the counter for 5 to 10 minutes before serving. Straight out of the oven the sauce is thin and the enchiladas will slide apart when you lift them; a short rest lets everything set enough to plate cleanly. It is also the difference between tasting your dinner and burning the roof of your mouth. Loosen the edges with a spatula while it rests.

instructions.title: Finish with cold toppings
instructions.text: Drizzle the crema over the hot enchiladas in thin lines, then scatter the queso fresco, thin-sliced white onion and cilantro across the top. Fan the avocado slices along one side. The cold, sharp toppings against the hot, tangy sauce are the whole point, so do not skip them. Serve with a lime wedge and plenty of napkins.

tips: Make the salsa verde up to 4 days ahead; it improves overnight. It also freezes for 3 months in a zip-top bag laid flat.
Assemble the whole dish, cover, and refrigerate up to 24 hours before baking. Add 8 to 10 minutes to the bake time if it goes in cold.
If your tomatillos are very tart, blend in 1/4 of a peeled avocado or 2 tbsp of crema to round the sauce out without dulling the flavor.
Never use flour tortillas here. They turn gummy and pasty under sauce, and corn is what makes these taste right.
A rotisserie chicken makes this a 45-minute weeknight dinner. One bird gives you almost exactly the 3 cups of meat you need.
recipes.keyTemp: Bake until the center of the dish reaches 165°F (74°C) and the sauce bubbles at the edges. Any pre-cooked chicken filling must be reheated to that same 165°F (74°C).
recipes.pairing: Black beans, Mexican rice and a cold michelada, or a bright Sauvignon Blanc if you want wine.

recipes.title: Enchiladas Rojas with Guajillo Sauce
recipes.blurb: A real red chile sauce built from toasted guajillos and anchos, not chili powder from a jar. Learn this sauce and you have unlocked half of Mexican cooking.

items: 2 dried chiles de arbol, optional, for heat
3 cups (700 ml) hot water, for soaking
1 tbsp (15 ml) apple cider vinegar, plus more to taste
1 tsp (7 g) honey, optional, if the sauce tastes bitter
1 1/2 tsp (9 g) kosher salt, plus more to taste
1/4 cup (60 ml) neutral oil, for softening the tortillas
8 oz (225 g) Monterey Jack or Chihuahua cheese, shredded (about 2 cups)
1/2 white onion, sliced paper thin (about 1/2 cup / 70 g)

instructions.title: Clean the dried chiles
instructions.text: Wipe each guajillo and ancho with a damp paper towel to remove dust, then snap off the stems and tear the chiles open along one side. Shake out and discard the seeds and pull away the pale veins inside, which carry bitterness more than heat. Guajillos are the tannic, bright, slightly fruity backbone; anchos are the sweet, raisiny, dark ones. Together they give you a sauce with both brightness and depth.

instructions.title: Toast the chiles
instructions.text: Heat a dry comal or heavy skillet over medium heat and press the opened chiles flat against the surface for 15 to 20 seconds per side. They should soften slightly, turn a shade lighter, and release a smell like sweet tobacco and dried fruit. Do not let them darken or smoke — a scorched chile turns the entire sauce acrid and bitter, and there is no way to rescue it. If you want real heat, toast the 2 chiles de arbol alongside them for 10 seconds a side only, since small thin chiles scorch in half the time. Work in batches so you can watch every piece.

instructions.title: Rehydrate in hot water
instructions.text: Put the toasted chiles in a bowl, pour the 3 cups (700 ml) of very hot water over them, and set a small plate on top to keep them submerged. Soak for 20 to 25 minutes until they are completely soft and floppy like wet leather. Taste the soaking water: if it is pleasantly fruity, save 1 cup for blending, and if it is bitter, dump it and use plain water instead. Old chiles that have gone brittle and gray will taste bitter no matter what you do.

instructions.title: Blend the sauce smooth
instructions.text: Put the drained chiles, onion, garlic, oregano, cumin, cinnamon, vinegar and 1 cup of the soaking liquid in a blender and run it on high for a full 90 seconds. It needs longer than you think — the skins are tough and a short blend leaves gritty flecks. The sauce should be the color of dark brick and completely smooth. Add up to 1/4 cup more liquid if the blender is struggling.

instructions.title: Strain the sauce
instructions.text: Pour the blended sauce through a fine-mesh sieve set over a bowl, pressing hard with a rubber spatula and scraping the underside of the sieve. You will leave behind a few tablespoons of tough skin, and what passes through will be silky. This one extra minute is the difference between a professional-tasting sauce and a slightly gritty one. Do not skip it, even with a high-powered blender.

instructions.title: Fry the sauce
instructions.text: Heat the 2 tbsp oil in a saucepan over medium-high until it shimmers, then pour in the strained sauce — it will hiss and spatter hard, so use a splatter screen. Cook for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring constantly, until it darkens, thickens, and smells toasted rather than raw. Frying the chile puree in fat blooms the fat-soluble flavors and is the single most important step in the recipe. Add the chicken broth and 1 1/2 tsp salt and simmer 8 minutes more.

instructions.title: Taste and balance
instructions.text: Taste the finished sauce and adjust: if it is flat, add salt; if it is harsh, add another 1/2 tsp vinegar; if it is bitter, a pinch of sugar or 1 tsp of honey will pull it back. It should coat a spoon like heavy cream and taste deep, faintly sweet and gently earthy. Season the shredded chicken with 1/2 cup of it and toss to coat. Keep the rest warm over low heat.

instructions.title: Preheat and prep the dish
instructions.text: Heat the oven to 400°F (205°C) with a rack in the middle position. Ladle 3/4 cup of the red sauce over the bottom of a 9 x 13 in (23 x 33 cm) baking dish and spread it into an even film. That layer keeps the tortillas from cementing themselves to the dish. Line up the sauce, filling, cheese and dish so assembly goes quickly.

instructions.title: Soften the tortillas
instructions.text: Heat the 1/4 cup (60 ml) oil in a small skillet over medium and pass each tortilla through for about 10 seconds per side, until floppy and just barely puffed. This seals the tortilla so it absorbs sauce without disintegrating. Drain them on paper towels in a stack. If you skip this, you will be serving red chile soup with corn mush in it.

instructions.title: Dip, fill and roll
instructions.text: Dip each softened tortilla into the warm red sauce to coat both sides, then lay it flat and spoon about 1/4 cup of the seasoned chicken down the middle with a small pinch of cheese. Roll it up snugly and set it seam side down in the dish. Pack them side by side so they support each other and stay rolled. Twelve should fit in a single tight row.

instructions.title: Top and bake
instructions.text: Pour the remaining sauce evenly over the top, covering all the exposed tortilla ends, then scatter the shredded cheese across. Bake uncovered for 18 to 20 minutes, until the sauce bubbles at the edges and the cheese has melted with browned spots. The center should read 165°F (74°C). If you want more color, broil for 60 seconds at the end.

instructions.title: Rest and garnish
instructions.text: Let the dish rest for 8 minutes so the sauce thickens enough to hold the enchiladas together when you serve them. Drizzle with crema, then top with queso fresco, thin-sliced onion and cilantro. The cool creamy garnishes cut the deep, slightly bitter chile flavor and are not decoration. Serve with a wedge of lime and rice on the side.

tips: Buy dried chiles that are still flexible and smell fragrant when you bend them. Brittle chiles that crack like a potato chip are old and will taste dusty and bitter.
The red chile sauce is the workhorse of this chapter. Make a double batch and freeze half — it becomes the base for tamales, pozole and birria.
If you toast a chile too far and it smells sharp and burnt, throw it out. One scorched chile will ruin an entire pot of sauce.
Guajillo is mild, ancho is mild and sweet, and chiles de arbol are genuinely hot. Adjust heat with the arbols only, and start with one.
Wear gloves or wash your hands thoroughly with soap after handling the soaked chiles, and keep your fingers away from your eyes for a while.
recipes.keyTemp: Bake until the center of the dish hits 165°F (74°C) and the sauce is bubbling. Toast the dried chiles only until fragrant, about 15 to 20 seconds per side — any smoke means bitterness.
recipes.pairing: Refried beans, Mexican rice, and a dark Negra Modelo or a glass of Garnacha.

recipes.title: Elote, Mexican Street Corn
recipes.blurb: Charred corn slathered in a lime and crema dressing, rolled in salty cotija and dusted with chile. Fifteen minutes of work for the best thing on the grill.

items: 4 ears fresh corn, husked and silk removed
1/4 cup (60 g) Mexican crema or sour cream
1 tbsp (15 ml) fresh lime juice, plus 1 tsp finely grated zest
3/4 cup (85 g) cotija cheese, finely crumbled
1 tsp (2 g) chili powder or Tajin, plus more for dusting

instructions.title: Pick and prep the corn
instructions.text: Look for ears with tight green husks and moist, pale silk at the tip, which means they were picked recently. Pull the husks off and rub the remaining silk away with a dry paper towel, which grabs it better than your fingers do. Trim the stem end flat so the ear sits still on the grill. Pat each ear completely dry, because wet corn steams instead of charring.

instructions.title: Mix the dressing
instructions.text: Whisk the crema, mayonnaise, grated garlic, lime juice, lime zest and 1/4 tsp salt in a wide shallow bowl big enough to roll an ear of corn in. The mayonnaise is not a shortcut — its emulsified fat is what makes the coating cling to hot corn instead of sliding off. Taste it and add more lime if it feels heavy. Set it next to the grill along with the cotija on a second plate.

instructions.title: Heat the grill hot
instructions.text: Get a charcoal or gas grill to medium-high, around 450°F (230°C), with the grates scraped clean and lightly oiled. If you are indoors, heat a cast iron grill pan or a heavy skillet over medium-high for 4 minutes until a drop of water dances and vanishes. You need real heat to blister the kernels before the corn overcooks and goes chewy. Rub the ears with the 1 tbsp oil and the 1/2 tsp salt.

instructions.title: Char the corn
instructions.text: Lay the ears on the grill and cook for 10 to 12 minutes total, turning every 2 to 3 minutes with tongs. You are after individual kernels blackened in spots across roughly a quarter of the surface, with the rest deep yellow and glossy. Uniformly black corn is burnt and tastes like ash; uniformly yellow corn is boiled and boring. Listen for the occasional pop, which means the kernels are heating through.

instructions.title: Check for doneness
instructions.text: Corn carries no food-safety temperature, so judge it by texture: press a kernel with your thumbnail and it should give slightly and release a little milky juice rather than squirting thin water. The kernels should be plump and glossy and the cob too hot to hold bare-handed, roughly 150°F to 165°F (65°C to 74°C) if you push a thermometer into the center of a row. Fresh summer corn only needs to be warmed and charred, since it is perfectly good raw. Older supermarket corn wants the full 12 minutes to lose its starchy chew.

instructions.title: Skewer them while hot
instructions.text: Move the ears to a board and push a wooden skewer or a corn holder into the stem end of each one, using a folded towel to protect your hand. A handle is what makes elote street food rather than fork-and-knife food. Work fast, because the dressing clings best to corn that is still steaming. Do not let the corn sit and cool while you look for the cotija.

instructions.title: Roll in the dressing
instructions.text: Roll each hot ear through the crema mixture, using the back of a spoon to push the dressing into every gap between the kernel rows. You want a thin, even white coat over the whole ear, not thick globs on one side. The heat will loosen the dressing slightly, which is what helps it spread. Let the excess drip back into the bowl.

instructions.title: Coat in cotija
instructions.text: Immediately roll the dressed ear in the crumbled cotija spread on a plate, pressing gently so the cheese sticks in a heavy layer. Crumble the cotija finely first — big chunks fall off on the first bite and end up on the floor. Cotija is salty and dry, closer to a young Parmesan than to feta. If you cannot find it, Pecorino Romano grated fine is the best substitute.

instructions.title: Dust and serve
instructions.text: Dust each ear generously with chili powder or Tajin and the optional cayenne, then scatter the chopped cilantro over the top. Serve right away with lime wedges to squeeze over at the table, which brightens all that fat and salt. Elote is best within five minutes of coming off the grill. Put a stack of napkins out and warn people it is messy.

tips: No grill? Char the corn under a broiler 4 in (10 cm) from the element for 10 to 12 minutes, turning every 3 minutes, and you will get almost the same result.
To turn this into esquites, cut the charred kernels off the cob and toss them with the dressing, cotija and chile in a bowl. Serve it warm with a spoon and it travels far better to a party.
The dressing keeps for 5 days in the fridge and is excellent on grilled zucchini, sweet potatoes or a wedge of iceberg.
Tajin brings lime and salt along with the chile, so if you use it, cut the added salt in the dressing to a pinch.
Buy corn the same day you cook it. Sugars turn to starch fast, and day-old supermarket corn is noticeably less sweet.
recipes.keyTemp: Corn has no safety temperature — the cue is texture. Grill over a surface around 450°F (230°C) until the kernels are blistered in spots, plump, and release milky juice under a thumbnail, which lands around 150°F to 165°F (65°C to 74°C) inside.
recipes.pairing: Anything off the grill, especially carne asada, plus a cold Mexican lager or a watermelon agua fresca.

recipes.title: Pozole Rojo with Pork and Hominy
recipes.blurb: A deep red chile broth with tender pork and chewy hominy, finished at the table with cabbage, radish and lime. It is Mexico's great celebration soup and it feeds a crowd.

items: 3 lb (1.35 kg) boneless pork shoulder, cut into 2 in (5 cm) chunks
1 lb (450 g) pork neck bones or country-style ribs, for body
1 tbsp (14 g) kosher salt, plus more to taste
2 dried chiles de arbol, optional, for heat
3 cups (700 ml) hot water, for soaking
2 cans (25 oz / 700 g each) white hominy, drained and rinsed
1 tsp (6 g) kosher salt, plus more to taste
3 cups (210 g) green cabbage, shredded thin
8 radishes, sliced paper thin (about 1 cup / 115 g)
1/2 white onion, finely diced (about 3/4 cup / 110 g)
2 tsp (2 g) dried Mexican oregano, for sprinkling
1 tsp (2 g) chile piquin or chili powder

instructions.title: Start the pork simmering
instructions.text: Put the pork shoulder chunks, neck bones, onion halves, 8 garlic cloves, bay leaves, 1 tbsp oregano and 1 tbsp salt in a large stockpot and cover with the 14 cups (3.3 L) water. Bring it to a boil over high heat, then immediately drop the heat to low so it barely simmers. A rolling boil emulsifies the fat and turns the broth cloudy and greasy instead of clear and clean. You want a bubble breaking the surface every second or two, no more.

instructions.title: Skim the foam
instructions.text: For the first 15 minutes, gray foam will rise to the surface — skim it off with a wide spoon or a small ladle and discard it. That foam is coagulated protein and it makes the finished broth murky and slightly bitter if you stir it back in. Once the foam stops forming and the surface is clear, partially cover the pot. Let it simmer for 2 hours while you make the chile paste.

instructions.title: Clean and toast the chiles
instructions.text: Wipe the guajillos and anchos with a damp towel, snap off the stems, tear them open and shake out the seeds and pale veins. Press them flat on a dry comal or skillet over medium heat for 15 to 20 seconds per side, until they smell like sweet dried fruit and tobacco. The instant you see wisps of smoke or the color going dark, they are burnt and the whole pot will taste bitter. Toast the arbols for only 10 seconds; they scorch fast.

instructions.title: Rehydrate the chiles
instructions.text: Cover the toasted chiles with the 3 cups (700 ml) hot water in a bowl and weigh them down with a plate so they stay under. Soak for 20 to 25 minutes until they are completely limp and soft, like wet leather. Taste the soaking liquid — if it is fruity and pleasant, reserve 1 1/2 cups of it for blending; if it is bitter, discard it and use fresh water. The chiles should tear easily between your fingers when they are ready.

instructions.title: Blend and strain the paste
instructions.text: Blend the drained chiles with the 4 garlic cloves, quartered onion, cumin, 1 tsp oregano and 1 1/2 cups of soaking liquid on high for a full 90 seconds until absolutely smooth. Pour it through a fine-mesh sieve into a bowl, pressing hard with a spatula to force everything but the tough skins through. Straining is what separates a silky red broth from a gritty one. You should have about 2 1/2 cups of smooth red paste.

instructions.title: Fry the chile paste
instructions.text: Heat the 2 tbsp oil in a skillet over medium-high until it shimmers, then add the strained paste all at once — it will spit, so use a splatter guard. Fry for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring constantly, until the paste darkens noticeably and thickens to the texture of tomato paste. This step blooms the chiles' fat-soluble flavors and removes the raw, dusty taste. It should smell rich and toasted, never sharp.

instructions.title: Check the pork
instructions.text: After 2 hours, test a chunk of pork shoulder with a fork — it should yield with almost no pressure and shred at the edges, at an internal temperature around 195°F (91°C). If it is still firm, give it another 20 to 30 minutes and check again. Lift out the neck bones and discard them along with the onion halves and bay leaves. Skim the fat off the top of the broth with a ladle, saving 2 tbsp of it if you want extra richness.

instructions.title: Marry the chile and the broth
instructions.text: Stir the fried chile paste into the pot and watch the broth turn a deep, glowing brick red. Simmer uncovered for 20 minutes so the flavors knit together and the broth reduces slightly. Taste it now and start seasoning — this is a big pot and it will take more salt than you expect, probably another 1 to 2 tsp. It should taste rounded and savory with a slow chile warmth, not sharp.

instructions.title: Add the hominy
instructions.text: Drain and rinse the canned hominy well under cold water to wash off the tinny canning liquid, then stir it into the pot. Simmer for another 20 to 25 minutes so the kernels soften slightly and drink up the red broth. Properly cooked hominy is chewy and springy with a faint sweet corn flavor, never mushy. If the broth has reduced too far, add 1 cup of hot water.

instructions.title: Shred the pork
instructions.text: Lift the pork chunks out with a slotted spoon onto a board and pull them into large, rough shreds with two forks, discarding any hard lumps of fat. Return the shredded meat to the pot and let it warm through for 5 minutes. Shredding after cooking, rather than before, keeps the pieces juicy instead of letting them dry out in the broth. Taste one last time for salt.

instructions.title: Set up the garnish table
instructions.text: Put the shredded cabbage, sliced radishes, diced onion, cilantro, lime wedges, oregano and chile piquin in separate small bowls and set them all in the middle of the table. Pozole is only half made in the pot; the cold crunchy garnishes are what make it come alive. Everyone builds their own bowl, and there is no wrong combination. Warm the tostadas in a 350°F (175°C) oven for 3 minutes.

instructions.title: Serve it very hot
instructions.text: Ladle the pozole into wide bowls, making sure each one gets plenty of pork, hominy and broth. Encourage everyone to crush oregano between their palms over the bowl and squeeze in lime before the first bite. The soup should be steaming hot, because it cools fast once the cold cabbage goes in. Serve tostadas on the side for dipping and crumbling.

tips: Pozole is famously better on day two. Make it a day ahead, chill it overnight, lift off the solid fat cap, and reheat gently — the chile flavor deepens noticeably.

Dried hominy is traditional and better, but it needs an overnight soak and 2 to 3 hours of its own cooking. Canned hominy is a perfectly respectable shortcut and what most home cooks in Mexico use now.
For pozole de pollo, swap in 3 lb (1.35 kg) of bone-in chicken thighs and cut the simmer to 45 minutes, pulling them at 175°F (79°C) for shreddable dark meat.
If the broth tastes bitter, one of your chiles scorched during toasting. A teaspoon of honey and an extra pinch of salt will mask it, but next time pull the chiles the second they smell fragrant.
Freeze leftovers without the garnishes in quart containers for up to 3 months. Add fresh cabbage and radish when you reheat.
recipes.keyTemp: Simmer the pork to about 195°F (91°C), far past the 145°F (63°C) plus 3-minute rest that pork needs for safety, so the collagen melts and the meat shreds. Serve the soup steaming at 165°F (74°C) or above.
recipes.pairing: Warm tostadas or a bolillo on the side, with a cold Mexican lager or a bright hibiscus agua fresca.
