recipes.title: Skillet Chicken Quesadillas
recipes.blurb: A crackling, blistered tortilla with a molten cheese seal and just enough seasoned chicken inside. Done right, a quesadilla is not lazy food at all.

items: 1 lb (450 g) boneless skinless chicken thighs, cut into 1/2 in (1.3 cm) pieces
1/2 white onion, thinly sliced (about 1 cup / 150 g)
1 poblano chile, seeded and sliced into thin strips
1 tsp (6 g) kosher salt, plus a pinch for the vegetables
12 oz (340 g) Oaxaca or Monterey Jack cheese, shredded (about 3 cups)
4 tbsp (57 g, half a stick) unsalted butter, softened
1/2 cup (120 ml) Mexican crema or sour cream
1 cup (240 ml) salsa or pico de gallo

instructions.title: Shred your own cheese
instructions.text: Buy Oaxaca or Monterey Jack in a block and shred it yourself on the large holes of a box grater. Pre-shredded cheese is dusted with potato starch and cellulose to keep it from clumping, and that coating makes it melt into a grainy, oily mess. Freshly shredded cheese melts into a smooth, stretchy sheet that glues the quesadilla shut. Keep it cold until the moment you build.

instructions.title: Season the chicken
instructions.text: Toss the diced chicken thighs with the cumin, chili powder, oregano, 1 tsp salt and pepper in a bowl until every piece is coated. Let it sit for 10 minutes while you slice the vegetables so the salt starts penetrating. Thighs are worth using over breast here because they stay juicy even after they go back into a hot skillet inside the quesadilla. Cut the pieces small so they lie flat and do not tear the tortilla.

instructions.title: Cook the chicken hot
instructions.text: Heat the 1 tbsp oil in a 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium-high until it shimmers, then add the chicken in a single layer and leave it undisturbed for 3 minutes. It should sizzle steadily and hard, not gently — that first contact is where the browning happens. Stir and cook 3 to 4 minutes more until the pieces are golden and register 165°F (74°C) on a thermometer. Scrape it all onto a plate.

instructions.title: Soften the onion and poblano
instructions.text: Add the sliced onion and poblano strips to the same pan with a pinch of salt and cook over medium-high for 5 to 6 minutes, stirring occasionally. You want them softened and streaked with brown at the edges, with the poblano just losing its raw grassiness. The browned bits left from the chicken will lift off the pan and season the vegetables. Return the chicken to the pan, add the lime juice, toss and turn off the heat.

instructions.title: Drain the filling
instructions.text: Tip the filling into a bowl and let it sit for a minute, then pour off any liquid that collects at the bottom. Wet filling is the number one cause of soggy quesadillas — the steam has nowhere to go and turns the tortilla limp. The filling should look glossy but not swimming. Stir the cilantro through it now.

instructions.title: Build with cheese on both sides
instructions.text: Lay a tortilla flat and scatter about 1/3 cup of shredded cheese over the entire surface, then spread a quarter of the chicken filling over one half only. Top the filling with another 1/3 cup of cheese and fold the bare half over. Cheese on both the bottom and the top of the filling is what welds the quesadilla into one piece instead of letting it fall open. Press the half-moon gently flat with your palm.

instructions.title: Butter the outside
instructions.text: Spread a thin film of the softened butter over the top surface of the folded quesadilla, using about 1/2 tbsp per side — 4 quesadillas buttered on both sides is where the 4 tbsp goes. Butter browns more evenly than oil and gives you that blistered, freckled crust with a nutty flavor. Do not use so much that it pools in the pan and fries the tortilla greasy. A thin swipe is all it takes.

instructions.title: Griddle low and slow
instructions.text: Wipe the skillet clean and set it over medium-low heat, then lay the quesadilla in butter side down and cook for 3 to 4 minutes. Medium-low is the key: the tortilla needs time for the cheese in the center to melt completely before the outside burns. It should hiss quietly, not crackle aggressively. Butter the exposed top side while the first side cooks. One skillet holds one quesadilla, so budget about 7 minutes each and hold the finished ones in a warm oven.

instructions.title: Flip and finish
instructions.text: Slide a wide spatula fully under the quesadilla and flip it in one confident motion, supporting the folded edge with your other hand. Cook the second side for 3 minutes until it is deep golden with dark blistered spots and the cheese is visibly molten at the seam. Press down gently with the spatula once to seal it. Cook the remaining quesadillas the same way.

instructions.title: Rest, then cut
instructions.text: Move each finished quesadilla to a cutting board and let it sit for 2 minutes before cutting. Molten cheese needs that moment to set up just slightly, or it all runs out the second the knife goes through. Cut each into 3 wedges with a large sharp knife or a pizza wheel, pressing straight down rather than sawing. Serve immediately with crema, salsa, avocado and lime.

tips: The Mexican street version uses corn tortillas folded around Oaxaca cheese and griddled dry. Try it once — it is a completely different and arguably better thing.
Any leftover braise from this chapter turns this into a great quesadilla: carnitas, tinga or birria all work. Drain them well first.
Keep finished quesadillas crisp in a 200°F (95°C) oven on a wire rack while you cook the rest. Never stack them, or the steam softens the crust.
If cheese leaks and burns in the pan, wipe the skillet clean between quesadillas. Burnt cheese turns bitter and blackens the next one.
For a make-ahead lunch, cook the filling up to 3 days in advance and refrigerate it. Assembly and griddling take under 10 minutes.
recipes.keyTemp: Cook the chicken to 165°F (74°C) before it goes into the quesadilla. Griddle over medium-low so the cheese fully melts, which takes 3 to 4 minutes per side.
recipes.pairing: Guacamole and chips, plus a lime agua fresca or an ice-cold Mexican lager.

recipes.title: Loaded Sheet Pan Nachos
recipes.blurb: Layered so every single chip gets cheese, beef and beans, then baked until it all fuses together. The trick is building it in two layers instead of one big pile.

items: 1/2 white onion, finely diced (about 3/4 cup / 110 g)
12 oz (340 g) sturdy tortilla chips, restaurant style
12 oz (340 g) sharp cheddar, shredded (about 3 cups)
8 oz (225 g) Monterey Jack, shredded (about 2 cups)
1 can (15 oz / 425 g) black beans, drained and rinsed
1/2 cup (75 g) pickled jalapeno slices, drained
1 1/2 cups (250 g) pico de gallo, drained
1/2 cup (120 ml) Mexican crema or sour cream

instructions.title: Heat the oven and pan
instructions.text: Set the oven to 400°F (205°C) with a rack in the upper third and line a rimmed sheet pan, about 13 x 18 in (33 x 46 cm), with parchment or foil. The upper rack gets the cheese browning without overcooking the chips underneath. Have every topping prepped and within arm's reach before anything goes in the oven, because nachos go from perfect to sad in about four minutes. Shred your own cheese from a block for a smoother melt.

instructions.title: Brown the beef properly
instructions.text: Heat a 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium-high and add the ground beef, breaking it into large chunks with a wooden spoon and then leaving it alone for 3 minutes. Letting it sit undisturbed builds a browned crust, which is where the flavor lives — constant stirring just steams gray meat. Add the onion and cook 4 minutes more, breaking the beef into smaller pieces. Stir in the garlic in the last 30 seconds.

instructions.title: Season and reduce
instructions.text: Sprinkle in the chili powder, cumin, oregano, smoked paprika and 1 tsp salt and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant, which toasts the spices in the hot fat. Add the 1/3 cup (80 ml) water and simmer for 2 to 3 minutes until the liquid has reduced to a glaze that clings to the meat. Ground beef must reach 160°F (71°C) to be safe, and this simmer takes it comfortably past that. The pan should look glossy, not soupy.

instructions.title: Drain the fat
instructions.text: Tilt the pan and spoon off all but about 1 tbsp of the rendered fat, or drain the meat in a sieve set over a bowl. Excess grease pools at the bottom of the sheet pan and turns the lower chips into a soggy raft. This is the step that separates good nachos from greasy ones. Taste the beef and adjust the salt now, while you still can.

instructions.title: Drain the wet toppings too
instructions.text: Tip the pico de gallo into a fine-mesh sieve and let it drain for 5 minutes, and shake the black beans and jalapenos dry. Water is the enemy of a crisp chip, and tomatoes hold a surprising amount of it. Set the drained toppings aside; the pico goes on cold at the end, never into the oven. Pat the beans dry with a paper towel if they still look wet.

instructions.title: Lay the first layer
instructions.text: Spread half the tortilla chips over the sheet pan in a single overlapping layer, edge to edge. Do not pile them into a mound — the whole point of a sheet pan is that every chip touches the heat. Choose thick, sturdy restaurant-style chips, since thin ones snap under a single spoonful of beef. A single flat layer is the foundation of the whole build.

instructions.title: Build layer one
instructions.text: Scatter half the beef, half the black beans and half of both cheeses over that first layer of chips, distributing them so no chip is left bare and none is buried. Layering matters more than quantity: two thin layers beat one thick pile every time. Cover the corners as generously as the middle, since those are the chips people fight over. Add half the pickled jalapenos.

instructions.title: Build layer two
instructions.text: Spread the remaining chips over the top, then repeat with the rest of the beef, beans, both cheeses and jalapenos. The second layer of cheese should be a little heavier than the first, because that top layer is what browns and blisters. Press the whole thing down gently with your palms so it holds together. Do not add anything fresh yet.

instructions.title: Bake until it fuses
instructions.text: Bake for 8 to 10 minutes, until the cheese is completely melted, bubbling at the edges, and just starting to brown in spots. Check at 8 minutes and pull it the moment the cheese stops looking wet and starts looking glossy. Overbaking dries the chips out and makes the cheese oily and separated. If you want more color, broil for exactly 60 seconds while watching it.

instructions.title: Top cold and serve on the pan
instructions.text: Pull the pan out and immediately scatter the drained pico de gallo, diced avocado, cilantro and scallions over the top, then drizzle the crema in thin zigzags from a spoon or a squeeze bottle. The contrast between the hot melted layer and the cold fresh toppings is what makes nachos good. Serve directly from the sheet pan with lime wedges. Eat within ten minutes, standing up, with your hands.

tips: Two thin layers instead of one deep pile is the entire secret. Every chip gets a topping and nothing steams into mush at the bottom.
Swap the ground beef for 2 cups of leftover carnitas, tinga or birria and these become genuinely special.
Never bake the tomatoes, avocado or crema. Anything fresh goes on after the pan leaves the oven, or it turns hot and slimy.
Cook the beef up to 3 days ahead and refrigerate it. Reheat it in a skillet before layering so it does not cool the cheese down.
For vegetarian nachos, double the black beans and add 1 cup of roasted sweet potato cubes or sauteed poblano strips in place of the beef.
recipes.keyTemp: Ground beef must reach 160°F (71°C) to be safe — check it in the pan before layering. Bake at 400°F (205°C) just until the cheese bubbles, 8 to 10 minutes.
recipes.pairing: A pitcher of margaritas or a cold lager, with extra guacamole and salsa on the side.

recipes.title: Red Chile Pork Tamales
recipes.blurb: Fluffy masa wrapped in corn husks around slow-braised pork in guajillo sauce, steamed until they slide clean out of the wrapper. Make them with someone you like, because it goes faster with two.

items: 3 lb (1.35 kg) boneless pork shoulder, cut into 3 in (8 cm) chunks
8 dried guajillo chiles (about 2 oz / 55 g), stemmed and seeded
4 dried ancho chiles (about 2 oz / 55 g), stemmed and seeded
3 cups (700 ml) hot water, for soaking the chiles
1 tsp (6 g) kosher salt, for the chile sauce, plus more to taste
4 cups (500 g) masa harina for tamales, such as Maseca
1 1/3 cups (280 g) lard, at room temperature
3 1/2 cups (830 ml) warm pork broth, from the braise, plus more as needed
36 dried corn husks (about 8 oz / 225 g), for 24 tamales plus tears
12 cups (2.8 L) hot water, for soaking husks
4 cups (950 ml) water, for the steamer

instructions.title: Braise the pork
instructions.text: Put the pork chunks, onion, garlic, bay leaves and 1 tbsp salt in a large pot with the 8 cups (1.9 L) water, bring to a boil, then lower to a bare simmer. Skim the gray foam off during the first 15 minutes so the broth stays clean. Simmer partially covered for 2 hours, until the pork shreds under fork pressure at about 195°F (91°C). Reserve every drop of the broth — you need 3 1/2 cups of it for the masa and another 1 1/2 cups for the chile sauce, and it is what makes homemade tamales taste like tamales.

instructions.title: Soak the corn husks
instructions.text: While the pork cooks, submerge the corn husks in the 12 cups (2.8 L) of hot water in a large bowl or clean sink, weighing them down with a plate. Soak for at least 30 minutes, until they are completely pliable and unfold without cracking. Rinse each one and rub off any grit or corn silk, then shake off the excess water. Tear 6 or 8 of the smaller husks lengthwise into thin strips to use as ties.

instructions.title: Toast and rehydrate the chiles
instructions.text: Press the stemmed, seeded guajillos and anchos flat on a dry comal over medium heat for 15 to 20 seconds per side, until they smell sweet and toasty. Pull them the instant they release their aroma; a chile that smokes has burned and will make the whole batch bitter. Cover them with 3 cups (700 ml) of hot water and soak 20 minutes until fully soft. Weigh them down with a plate so they stay submerged.

instructions.title: Make the red chile sauce
instructions.text: Blend the drained chiles with 1 1/2 cups of the pork broth, the cumin, oregano and vinegar for a full 90 seconds until perfectly smooth, then push it through a fine-mesh sieve to remove the skins. Heat the 2 tbsp oil in a skillet over medium-high and fry the strained sauce for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until it darkens and thickens. Frying is not optional — it turns raw chile puree into a deep, rounded sauce. Stir in the 1 tsp salt, taste, and add more until the sauce tastes seasoned on its own.

instructions.title: Shred and sauce the pork
instructions.text: Pull the cooled pork into rough shreds with two forks, discarding hard fat, and stir it into the red chile sauce in a bowl. You want the pork glossy and well coated but not swimming, so add sauce a ladle at a time until it looks right. Taste and season aggressively — the masa around it is mild, so the filling has to carry the flavor for both. Let it cool completely before assembling, or it will melt the masa.

instructions.title: Whip the lard
instructions.text: Beat the 1 1/3 cups (280 g) of room-temperature lard in a stand mixer with the paddle on medium-high for 4 to 5 minutes, until it is white, fluffy and roughly doubled in volume, like frosting. This is the step that decides whether your tamales are light or dense, so do not shorten it. Cold lard will not whip; leave it out for an hour first. Scrape the bowl down twice as you go.

instructions.title: Build the masa
instructions.text: In a separate bowl, whisk the masa harina, baking powder and 2 tsp salt together. Add this to the whipped lard in three additions, alternating with the 3 1/2 cups of warm pork broth, and beat on medium for 5 minutes after the last addition. The finished masa should look like thick, spreadable hummus and hold a soft peak on a spoon. Masa harina varies in how much it drinks, so start here and beat in more warm broth 2 tbsp at a time if it is stiff — you are aiming for the texture, not a number.

instructions.title: Test the masa float
instructions.text: Drop a 1/2 tsp ball of masa into a cup of cold water. If it floats within a few seconds, enough air has been beaten in and your tamales will be fluffy. If it sinks, keep beating for another 2 to 3 minutes and test again. This old kitchen test is the only reliable way to know before you have wrapped two dozen tamales.

instructions.title: Spread the masa
instructions.text: Lay a soaked husk flat with the wide end toward you and the smooth side up. Spread about 1/4 cup (60 g) of masa into a rectangle roughly 4 x 3 in (10 x 8 cm), leaving a 2 in (5 cm) border at the narrow end and about 1/2 in (1.3 cm) at the sides. Use the back of a spoon or an offset spatula and keep the layer about 1/4 in (6 mm) thick. Too thick and the tamale is stodgy; too thin and it tears.

instructions.title: Fill and fold
instructions.text: Spoon about 3 tbsp of the red chile pork down the center of the masa in a line, which is what divides 3 lb of braised shoulder evenly across 24 tamales. Fold one long side of the husk over so the masa wraps around the filling, then fold the other side over it like closing a book. Fold the narrow empty end up against the seam and tie it loosely with a strip of husk if you like. Loose is important — the masa expands as it steams and a tight tamale bursts.

instructions.title: Load the steamer
instructions.text: Set a steamer rack in a tall stockpot and add the 4 cups (950 ml) water, keeping the level below the rack. Stand the tamales upright with the folded end down and the open end up, packed snugly enough to support each other but not crushed. Tuck a few extra husks around and over the top, cover with the lid, and bring the water to a boil. If they will not stand, lay them flat with the seam side down in layers.

instructions.title: Steam 75 to 90 minutes
instructions.text: Steam over medium heat for 75 to 90 minutes, checking the water level every 30 minutes and adding boiling water down the side as needed. If the pot ever runs dry the tamales scorch and the whole batch is lost, so set a timer. The tamales are done when the masa pulls cleanly away from the husk and holds its shape rather than smearing. Test one at 75 minutes; if it sticks, give the batch another 15.

instructions.title: Rest before eating
instructions.text: Turn off the heat and let the tamales sit in the covered pot for 15 minutes before unwrapping. This rest lets the masa firm up, and a tamale opened straight off the steam will be gummy even when it is perfectly cooked. Serve them in their husks and let everyone unwrap their own. Pass extra red chile sauce and crema at the table.

tips: Tamales are a group project. Set up an assembly line with one person spreading masa, one filling and one folding, and 24 tamales take 30 minutes instead of 90.
Look for masa harina labeled for tamales, which is coarser than the kind for tortillas. Regular Maseca works, but the texture is a little finer than traditional.
The float test is the real quality control. Under-whipped masa gives you dense, heavy tamales and no amount of extra steaming will fix it.
Tamales freeze better than almost anything. Cool them completely, freeze in a bag for up to 6 months, and resteam from frozen for 20 to 25 minutes.
Vegetarian version: fill with roasted poblano strips and Oaxaca cheese, and swap the lard for vegetable shortening plus vegetable broth.
recipes.keyTemp: Braise the pork to about 195°F (91°C) so it shreds easily, well past the 145°F (63°C) safety minimum. The tamales are done when the masa peels cleanly from the husk after 75 to 90 minutes of steaming.
recipes.pairing: Champurrado or Mexican hot chocolate on a cold morning, or a cold lager and a bowl of pozole for a party.

recipes.title: Sizzling Skillet Steak Fajitas
recipes.blurb: Charred skirt steak and blistered peppers cooked in the same screaming-hot skillet, brought to the table still sizzling. The smell alone is worth the smoke alarm risk.

items: 1 1/2 lb (680 g) skirt steak, trimmed and cut into 6 in (15 cm) lengths
1/4 cup (60 ml) fresh lime juice (about 3 limes)
2 bell peppers, one red and one green, sliced into 1/2 in (1.3 cm) strips
1 poblano chile, sliced into 1/2 in (1.3 cm) strips
1 large yellow onion, sliced into 1/2 in (1.3 cm) half-moons (about 10 oz / 285 g)
1/2 cup (120 ml) Mexican crema or sour cream

instructions.title: Mix the marinade
instructions.text: Whisk the 1/4 cup (60 ml) lime juice, 3 tbsp oil, garlic, Worcestershire, cumin, chili powder, oregano, 2 tsp salt and pepper in a bowl until it looks slightly creamy. The Worcestershire brings a savory, almost beefy depth that lime and spices alone cannot give you. Taste it and expect it to be sharp and salty, since only a coating stays on the meat. Reserve 2 tbsp of it in a separate cup for the vegetables later.

instructions.title: Marinate one hour, not four
instructions.text: Put the steak in a zip-top bag with the marinade, press out the air, and refrigerate for exactly 1 hour, or up to 2 at the outside. Lime juice is aggressive, and past a couple of hours it starts cooking the surface of the meat into something chalky and mealy. One hour is enough to season the outside and start tenderizing. Take the steak out 20 minutes before cooking so it is not fridge-cold.

instructions.title: Cut the vegetables uniformly
instructions.text: Slice the bell peppers, poblano and onion into strips about 1/2 in (1.3 cm) wide so they cook at the same rate. Thin slices go limp before they char and thick ones stay raw in the middle. Keep the onion in half-moons rather than rings so the pieces stay intact when you toss them. Have everything cut and within reach before the pan goes on, because this cooks fast.

instructions.title: Heat the skillet hard
instructions.text: Set a 12 in (30 cm) cast iron skillet over high heat for a full 5 minutes, until a drop of water evaporates on contact with a hiss. Cast iron is the right pan because it holds enough stored heat to keep searing when cold meat hits it. Turn on the vent hood, crack a window, and put a towel over the smoke detector if you have to. This is a genuinely smoky dish.

instructions.title: Dry the steak
instructions.text: Lift the steak out of the marinade and scrape off the garlic bits with the back of a knife, since they will scorch black in a pan this hot. Blot both sides thoroughly dry with paper towels. Any surface moisture has to boil away before browning can start, and in the 3 minutes that takes, the steak overcooks. A dry surface is the whole game with a thin cut.

instructions.title: Sear the steak
instructions.text: Lay the steak in the dry skillet — the oil clinging from the marinade is plenty — and sear undisturbed for 3 minutes. It should roar the moment it lands, not whisper; a quiet pan means it was not hot enough and the steak is stewing in its own juice. Flip once and cook 2 to 3 minutes more, then pull it the instant an instant-read thermometer in the thickest part reads 130°F (54°C), which is the pull temp for medium-rare, not the finished temp. Carryover heat carries it another 5 degrees while it rests, so 130°F off the heat lands at about 135°F (57°C) on the plate. Work in two batches if the pieces overlap, because crowding steams the meat gray.

instructions.title: Rest the steak
instructions.text: Move the steak to a cutting board and tent it loosely with foil for 10 minutes while you cook the vegetables. The internal temperature will drift up to about 135°F (57°C) and the juices will settle back into the fibers. Cutting into skirt steak straight off the heat costs you a puddle of juice on the board. Do not skip this, even though the pan is calling.

instructions.title: Blister the vegetables
instructions.text: Add the 2 tbsp oil to the same skillet, still over high heat, then dump in the onions and peppers with the 1 tsp salt. Spread them into a single layer and let them sit for 2 minutes without stirring so they char, then toss and repeat for 6 to 8 minutes total. You want blistered black edges with the centers still crisp-tender, not soft, wet stewed peppers. The browned steak fond on the pan bottom will lift into them.

instructions.title: Deglaze with the reserved marinade
instructions.text: Pour the reserved 2 tbsp of marinade and the 1 tbsp lime juice into the hot skillet and scrape the bottom hard with a wooden spoon for 30 seconds. Everything stuck to the pan will release and coat the vegetables in a glaze that tastes like the steak you just cooked. This is why you set that 2 tbsp aside in a separate cup before the raw beef ever went into the bag — marinade that has held raw meat is never safe to add at the end unless it is boiled hard for a full minute first. Let it bubble away to almost nothing, then turn off the heat.

instructions.title: Warm the tortillas
instructions.text: Toast the flour tortillas one at a time on a dry comal or in a skillet over medium-high for 20 to 30 seconds per side, until they puff slightly and show a few brown freckles. Stack them in a clean towel or a tortilla warmer so they steam soft. Warm tortillas fold without cracking and taste worlds better than cold ones. Do this while the steak rests.

instructions.title: Slice against the grain
instructions.text: Find the direction of the long muscle fibers in the skirt steak and slice straight across them at a slight angle, into strips about 1/4 in (6 mm) thick. Slicing with the grain leaves you chewing long tough strands, and this cut is completely unforgiving about it. Pour any juices from the board back over the sliced meat. Season with a final pinch of salt.

instructions.title: Serve it sizzling
instructions.text: Return the sliced steak to the hot skillet with the peppers and toss once, letting everything sizzle together for 30 seconds. Carry the skillet straight to the table on a trivet while it is still crackling and steaming. Serve with the warm tortillas, guacamole, crema, pico de gallo and lime wedges so everyone builds their own. The sizzle only lasts a minute, so have everyone seated.

tips: Skirt steak is the traditional cut and the best one. Flank is a good substitute but slice it even thinner, and avoid stew meat or sirloin tips, which never get tender.
Do not marinate longer than 2 hours. Long acidic marinades turn the outside of thin steak into a mealy gray band.
For a real restaurant sizzle, preheat a second cast iron skillet or a fajita platter in a 450°F (230°C) oven and transfer everything onto it right before serving.
Chicken fajitas work with the same marinade using 1 1/2 lb (680 g) of thighs, cooked to 165°F (74°C), about 5 to 6 minutes per side.
If your kitchen cannot handle the smoke, cook this on a grill over direct high heat with a cast iron pan for the vegetables. Same times, no alarms.
recipes.keyTemp: Pull skirt steak at 130°F (54°C) for medium-rare; it rises to about 135°F (57°C) while resting. If you swap in chicken, cook it fully to 165°F (74°C).
recipes.pairing: A frozen lime margarita or a cold Modelo, with Mexican rice and charro beans on the side.

recipes.title: Guacamole and Pico de Gallo
recipes.blurb: Chunky guacamole made in a bowl with a fork and a pico that actually tastes of tomato, not water. Two five-ingredient recipes that everything else in this chapter leans on.

items: 1 lb (450 g) ripe Roma tomatoes (about 5), seeded and diced 1/4 in (6 mm)
1/2 white onion, finely diced (about 3/4 cup / 110 g)
1 serrano chile, seeded and minced (about 1 tbsp / 8 g)
3/4 tsp (5 g) kosher salt, plus more to taste
3 large ripe Hass avocados (about 1 1/2 lb / 680 g total)
1/4 white onion, very finely diced (about 1/3 cup / 50 g)
1 serrano chile, seeded and minced (about 1 tbsp / 8 g)
1 tsp (6 g) kosher salt, plus more to taste
1/4 cup (30 g) crumbled cotija cheese, optional

instructions.title: Seed the tomatoes
instructions.text: Cut each Roma tomato in half lengthwise and scoop out the seeds and the watery gel with your thumb or a small spoon. That jelly is almost pure water, and leaving it in is exactly why homemade pico ends up sitting in a pink puddle. Dice the firm outer flesh into neat 1/4 in (6 mm) pieces. Roma tomatoes are the right choice because they are meaty and low in moisture.

instructions.title: Tame the raw onion
instructions.text: Dice the white onion small and even, then rinse it in a fine sieve under cold water for 20 seconds and shake it dry. Rinsing washes away the sulfur compounds that make raw onion taste harsh and linger on your breath, without touching the crunch or sweetness. This 20-second step makes a real difference in a raw salsa. Do the same for the onion going into the guacamole.

instructions.title: Mix and rest the pico
instructions.text: Combine the tomatoes, rinsed onion, minced serrano, cilantro, 2 tbsp lime juice and 3/4 tsp salt in a bowl and stir gently. Let it sit for 10 minutes so the salt draws out just enough juice to make a light dressing and the flavors get acquainted. Taste it after resting, not before — salt and lime read completely differently once everything has mingled. Drain off excess liquid if it looks watery.

instructions.title: Judge the serrano heat
instructions.text: Taste a tiny sliver of your serrano before adding it, because heat varies wildly from chile to chile even off the same plant. Scrape out the seeds and white veins for moderate heat, or leave some in if the chile is mild. Start with half and add the rest once you have tasted the finished bowl. It is the one thing here you cannot undo.

instructions.title: Pick and open the avocados
instructions.text: A ripe Hass avocado yields to gentle pressure near the stem and its little stem cap flicks off to reveal green, not brown. Halve each one around the pit, twist the halves apart, and strike the pit firmly with the heel of your knife to lift it out. Score the flesh in a crosshatch right in the skin and scoop it out with a spoon. Unripe avocados will never taste good, no matter what you add.

instructions.title: Build the guacamole base
instructions.text: Put the rinsed onion, minced serrano, cilantro and 1 tsp salt in the bowl first and mash them together with a fork or a molcajete before the avocado goes in. Grinding the aromatics with salt releases their oils and distributes them evenly instead of leaving pockets of raw onion. This is the traditional order and it makes a noticeably better guacamole. It takes 30 seconds.

instructions.title: Mash it chunky
instructions.text: Add the avocado and the 2 tbsp lime juice and mash with a fork just 8 to 10 times, leaving plenty of half-inch chunks intact. Guacamole should have texture you can feel — a food processor turns it into pale green baby food. The lime is doing two jobs here: seasoning and slowing the browning. Fold rather than stir once it starts coming together.

instructions.title: Season at the end
instructions.text: Taste the guacamole and adjust with salt a pinch at a time and lime a teaspoon at a time until it tastes bright rather than flat. Avocado is fatty and mild, so it swallows salt — most home cooks stop about half a teaspoon short. If it tastes dull, it needs salt; if it tastes heavy, it needs lime. Fold in 2 tbsp of the pico for extra brightness if you like.

instructions.title: Keep it green
instructions.text: If you are not serving right away, smooth the surface flat and press plastic wrap directly onto the guacamole so no air touches it, then refrigerate for up to 4 hours. Browning is oxidation, so contact with plastic works far better than the avocado-pit myth. Alternatively, pour a thin layer of cold water over the smoothed surface and pour it off before serving. Give it a stir and re-taste before it goes out.

instructions.title: Serve both together
instructions.text: Spoon the guacamole into a shallow bowl and the pico into another, and set them side by side with a big basket of tortilla chips. Sprinkle the guacamole with the optional cotija and set out lime wedges. Both should be made the day you serve them, and both are better at cool room temperature than straight from the fridge. Pull them out 15 minutes before eating.

tips: Ripen hard avocados in a paper bag with a banana for 1 to 2 days. Once ripe, refrigerating them buys you about 3 more days.
Pico de gallo is best within 4 hours. After that the tomatoes weep and the cilantro darkens, so make it the same day.
For a smokier guacamole, char the serrano and a couple of scallions over a flame until blistered before mincing them in.
White onion is the right onion for both of these. Yellow is too sweet and red bleeds pink into the guacamole.
Leftover pico is excellent stirred into scrambled eggs, spooned over grilled fish, or drained and used on the nachos in this chapter.
recipes.keyTemp: No cooking involved. The cue is texture: guacamole should stay chunky with visible half-inch pieces of avocado, and pico should be crisp and barely wet, never sitting in a pool of liquid.
recipes.pairing: Salty thick-cut tortilla chips and a cold beer, or as the cooling side to anything spicy in this chapter.

recipes.title: Queso Fundido with Chorizo
recipes.blurb: A skillet of melted Oaxaca cheese with spicy chorizo and blistered poblano, pulled apart with warm tortillas. It takes half an hour and disappears in ten minutes.

items: 8 oz (225 g) fresh Mexican pork chorizo, casings removed
1 poblano chile, seeded and cut into thin strips
1/2 white onion, thinly sliced (about 1 cup / 150 g)
12 oz (340 g) Oaxaca cheese, shredded or pulled into strands (about 3 cups)
4 oz (115 g) Monterey Jack, shredded (about 1 cup)
2 tbsp (30 ml) Mexican lager or whole milk
16 corn or flour tortillas, 6 in (15 cm)

instructions.title: Heat the oven
instructions.text: Set the oven to 425°F (220°C) with a rack in the upper third, and if you have a broiler you will want it ready too. A hot oven melts the cheese fast, which matters because slow melting gives the fat time to separate and pool. Have your tortillas, cilantro and salsa ready before the skillet goes in. Queso fundido waits for absolutely no one.

instructions.title: Pull the cheese into strands
instructions.text: Oaxaca cheese comes wound into a ball like a skein of yarn — unwind it and pull it into thin strands with your fingers rather than grating it. Pulled strands melt more evenly and give you the long stretchy pull this dish is famous for. Mix it with the shredded Monterey Jack, which is milder and helps keep the melt smooth. Never use pre-shredded bagged cheese here; the anti-caking starch turns the melt grainy.

instructions.title: Brown the chorizo
instructions.text: Squeeze the chorizo out of its casing into a cold 10 in (25 cm) cast iron skillet, set it over medium heat, and break it up with a wooden spoon. Cook for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until it is deeply browned in crumbles and the fat has run bright orange-red. Fresh Mexican chorizo is raw pork sausage and must reach 160°F (71°C), unlike cured Spanish chorizo. It should sizzle steadily, not scorch.

instructions.title: Drain most of the fat
instructions.text: Tip the skillet and spoon off all but about 1 tbsp of the rendered chorizo fat, or the finished queso will be a greasy orange slick. That single tablespoon is enough to cook the vegetables and season everything. Save the drained fat in a jar for frying eggs or potatoes, because it is delicious. Leave the browned crumbles in the pan.

instructions.title: Cook the poblano and onion
instructions.text: Add the poblano strips, sliced onion and 1/2 tsp salt to the skillet and cook over medium-high for 5 to 6 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the vegetables are softened with charred edges. The poblano should lose its raw grassy taste and turn silky. Add the sliced garlic for the final 30 seconds only, since it burns fast in a hot pan. Scrape any brown bits off the bottom as you stir.

instructions.title: Set aside the topping
instructions.text: Scoop about two-thirds of the chorizo and vegetable mixture out of the skillet onto a plate, leaving the rest spread across the bottom. You will scatter the reserved portion over the melted cheese at the end so it does not sink and disappear. Layering it this way means every scoop gets both cheese and chorizo. Wipe the skillet rim clean so nothing burns in the oven.

instructions.title: Add the cheese and liquid
instructions.text: Pile the mixed cheeses over the chorizo in the skillet in an even mound and drizzle the 2 tbsp of lager or milk over the top. That small amount of liquid helps the cheese melt into a cohesive, saucy mass rather than breaking into strings and oil. Do not add more than 2 tbsp or the queso will be soupy. Press the cheese down gently so it sits level.

instructions.title: Bake until molten
instructions.text: Slide the skillet into the 425°F (220°C) oven and bake for 6 to 8 minutes, until the cheese is completely melted and bubbling at the edges. Start checking at 6 minutes: the moment it goes from a solid mound to a shimmering molten pool, it is done. Overbaking is the classic mistake here — the proteins tighten, the fat separates, and you get a rubbery raft floating in grease. If you want brown spots, broil for 45 to 60 seconds only.

instructions.title: Warm the tortillas
instructions.text: While the cheese bakes, toast the tortillas on a dry comal or skillet over medium-high heat for 20 to 30 seconds per side until soft and lightly freckled. Stack them inside a clean kitchen towel or a tortilla warmer to keep the steam in. You need them ready the second the skillet comes out. Cold tortillas will chill the queso on contact.

instructions.title: Top and serve immediately
instructions.text: Scatter the reserved chorizo and vegetables over the molten cheese, sprinkle the cilantro on top, and carry the skillet straight to the table on a trivet. Serve with the warm tortillas, salsa verde and lime wedges, and have everyone scoop and roll their own. Queso fundido stays perfect for about eight minutes and then begins to set, so this is not a dish to plate up quietly in the kitchen. Warn everyone that the handle is blistering hot.

tips: Oaxaca cheese is the correct cheese and it is worth a trip. Low-moisture whole-milk mozzarella is the closest substitute; avoid cheddar, which breaks and goes oily.
If the queso sets before everyone is finished, put the skillet back in the oven for 2 to 3 minutes. It will re-melt once, though not twice.
For a vegetarian version, skip the chorizo and use 8 oz (225 g) of sliced mushrooms browned hard in 2 tbsp of oil, plus an extra poblano.
Fresh Mexican chorizo is raw and soft; Spanish chorizo is cured and firm. They are not interchangeable, and using the cured kind here leaves you with dry chips of sausage.
Prep the chorizo and vegetables up to 2 days ahead. Reheat them in the skillet, add the cheese, and bake when your guests arrive.
recipes.keyTemp: Fresh pork chorizo must reach 160°F (71°C) before the cheese goes in. Bake at 425°F (220°C) only until the cheese is molten and bubbling, 6 to 8 minutes, or it will break and turn greasy.
recipes.pairing: Cold Mexican lager or a michelada, served as the opener before carne asada or fajitas.

recipes.title: Beef Birria Tacos with Consomé
recipes.blurb: Chile-braised beef shredded into cheese-crisped tortillas, dipped in the ruby red consomé it cooked in. It is a long afternoon and the best taco you will ever make at home.

items: 3 lb (1.35 kg) boneless beef chuck roast, cut into 3 in (8 cm) chunks
2 lb (900 g) bone-in beef short ribs
8 dried guajillo chiles (about 2 oz / 55 g), stemmed and seeded
4 dried ancho chiles (about 2 oz / 55 g), stemmed and seeded
3 cups (700 ml) hot water, for soaking
2 tsp (12 g) kosher salt, plus more to taste
1 lb (450 g) Oaxaca or Monterey Jack cheese, shredded (about 4 cups)
1 white onion, finely diced (about 1 1/2 cups / 220 g)

instructions.title: Season the beef
instructions.text: Pat the chuck chunks and short ribs completely dry and season them all over with the 1 tbsp salt and 1 tsp pepper. Let them sit at room temperature for 20 minutes so the salt begins to penetrate and the surface dries further. The short ribs are not optional filler — their bones and connective tissue are what give the consomé its body and glossy lip-sticking texture. Chuck alone makes a thinner broth.

instructions.title: Sear in batches
instructions.text: Heat the 2 tbsp oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high until it just begins to shimmer, then sear the beef in two or three batches, 3 to 4 minutes per side. Each piece should be deeply browned and release from the pot on its own before you move it. Crowding drops the temperature and the meat steams gray, costing you the browned flavor that carries the whole braise. Set the seared beef aside on a plate.

instructions.title: Toast the dried chiles
instructions.text: Wipe out most of the fat, lower the heat to medium, and press the stemmed and seeded guajillos, anchos and arbols flat against the hot pot for 15 to 20 seconds per side. They should puff slightly, lighten in color, and smell like sweet dried fruit and tobacco. The second you see smoke or smell anything sharp, they have burned and the whole batch will taste bitter. Toast in batches so you can watch every chile.

instructions.title: Rehydrate the chiles
instructions.text: Move the toasted chiles to a bowl, pour the 3 cups (700 ml) of hot water over them, and hold them under with a small plate. Soak 20 to 25 minutes until they are completely soft and floppy. Taste the soaking liquid and reserve 1 1/2 cups if it is fruity, or discard it and use fresh water if it tastes bitter. Softened chiles blend smooth; stiff ones leave grit.

instructions.title: Char the tomatoes and aromatics
instructions.text: While the chiles soak, char the tomato halves, onion halves and garlic cloves in the same pot or a dry skillet over medium-high for 6 to 8 minutes, turning until blackened in spots. This char adds a smoky sweetness that raw vegetables cannot give you. The garlic will color fastest, so pull it after about 3 minutes. Let everything cool slightly before it goes into the blender.

instructions.title: Blend the adobo
instructions.text: Blend the drained chiles, charred tomatoes, onion, garlic, cinnamon stick, cloves, cumin, oregano, vinegar and 1 1/2 cups of soaking liquid on high for a full 2 minutes. Cinnamon and cloves are the signature of birria and they should be present but subtle, more warm than sweet. The adobo should be completely smooth and the color of dark garnet. Add a splash more liquid if the blender is laboring.

instructions.title: Strain the adobo
instructions.text: Push the blended adobo through a fine-mesh sieve into a bowl, pressing hard with a spatula and scraping the underside to get everything through. You will be left with a few tablespoons of tough chile skin and spice fragments to discard. A whole cinnamon stick will not fully break down, so this strain is what keeps the consomé silky rather than gritty. It takes two minutes and it matters.

instructions.title: Fry the adobo, then braise
instructions.text: Return the pot to medium-high, pour in the strained adobo, and fry it for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until it darkens and thickens like tomato paste. Add the beef broth, bay leaves and 2 tsp salt, then return the beef and any juices from the plate. Bring it to a simmer, cover, and either keep it at a bare simmer on the stove or slide it into a 325°F (163°C) oven. The liquid should just about cover the meat.

instructions.title: Braise until it shreds
instructions.text: Cook for 3 to 3 1/2 hours, checking at 3 hours, until the beef falls apart at the nudge of a fork and reads about 203°F (95°C) on a thermometer. Do not judge it by the clock alone — collagen breaks down on its own schedule, and a piece that is still tight needs another 30 minutes. The braise should bubble lazily, never boil. Underdone birria is stringy and tough, and the only cure is more time.

instructions.title: Rest and skim the fat
instructions.text: Turn off the heat and let the pot rest, uncovered, for 15 minutes so the fat rises and the meat relaxes. Skim the bright orange-red fat off the surface with a ladle and reserve every bit of it in a bowl — this is the birria fat you will dip the tortillas in, and it is the entire point of a quesabirria. You should end up with 1/2 to 3/4 cup. Do not throw it out.

instructions.title: Shred the beef and finish the consomé
instructions.text: Lift the beef out with a slotted spoon, pull the short rib meat off the bones, and shred everything into rough strands with two forks, discarding bones and hard fat. Taste the remaining broth — this is your consomé — and season it with salt until it is bright and savory, probably another 1 to 2 tsp. Moisten the shredded meat with about 1 cup of the consomé so it does not dry out. Ladle the rest into small bowls for dipping.

instructions.title: Griddle the quesabirria tacos
instructions.text: Heat a comal or large skillet over medium heat. Dip a tortilla into the reserved red fat so one side is coated, lay it fat side down on the griddle, and scatter about 3 tbsp of cheese over half of it. When the cheese melts, about 1 minute, add 1/4 cup of shredded beef, fold it over, and press gently with a spatula. Cook 1 to 2 minutes per side until the tortilla is crisp and lacquered deep red.

instructions.title: Serve with consomé for dipping
instructions.text: Stack three tacos per plate and top them with diced white onion and cilantro. Give each person a small bowl of hot consomé with a squeeze of lime and a pinch of onion and cilantro stirred in. The dipping is not a garnish, it is how the dish is eaten, so make sure everyone has enough. Serve immediately while the tortillas are still crackling.

tips: Birria is dramatically better the next day. Braise it a day ahead, refrigerate overnight, lift off the solid fat cap to use for griddling, and reheat the meat gently in its consomé.
Goat is the original meat for birria and lamb shoulder is a superb substitute. Both use the same adobo and the same timing.
The reserved red fat is what makes a quesabirria taco. If you skim it away or throw it out, you get a regular taco and miss the point entirely.
If your consomé tastes bitter, a chile scorched during toasting. Stir in 1 tsp of honey and a splash of vinegar to rebalance it, and be gentler with the comal next time.
Freeze the shredded meat and consomé together in quart containers for up to 3 months. It reheats perfectly and turns a Tuesday into an event.
recipes.keyTemp: Braise the beef to about 203°F (95°C), far past the 145°F (63°C) safety minimum, so the collagen melts into gelatin and the meat shreds with a fork. Judge by fork tenderness first, temperature second.
recipes.pairing: A michelada or a cold Victoria, with the consomé itself as the first course.
